issues.legal_issue: A customary holder of ancestral agricultural land may transfer it for consideration, and the transfer is not liable to be set aside by an heir unless it was for an immoral purpose.
material_facts: The land was ancestral agricultural land held by Jats of the relevant customary community.
The holder sold the land for consideration.
The holder’s sons and other reversionary heirs sought to have the sale declared void against them.
Although the heirs alleged an immoral purpose, the courts found that the sale was not for such a purpose.
The courts below found that the applicable custom permitted the holder to transfer the land, consistently with numerous earlier decisions.
issues.conclusion: The holder had customary power to transfer the ancestral land for consideration, and the sale was not liable to be set aside at the instance of his sons or other reversionary heirs because it was not for an immoral purpose.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on the Rohtak customary records, including the Riwaj-i-am recorded in Joseph’s Customary Law Manual and Tupper’s Statements of Customary Law, and on the consistent line of decisions recognizing the holder’s power, including Telu v. Chuni, Giani v. Tek Chand, Behari v. Bhola, Abdul Rafi Khan v. Lakshmi Chand, Ram Datt v. Khushi Ram, Pahlad Singh v. Sukhdev Singh, Sohan Lal v. Rati Ram, Suraj Mal v. Birju, and Sheoji v. Fajar Ali Khan. It held that Budal v. Kirpa Ram, which had taken a contrary view, had not been followed and was not a satisfactory basis for reviving that view.

rule.if: heir_challenge_to_transfer and customary_transfer_power and transfer_for_consideration and not immoral_purpose

predicates.heir_challenge_to_transfer: An heir seeks to have a holder’s transfer of ancestral land declared ineffective against the heir.
predicates.customary_transfer_power: The applicable custom permits the holder to transfer the ancestral land for consideration.
predicates.transfer_for_consideration: The holder transferred the land in exchange for consideration.
predicates.immoral_purpose: The transfer was made for an immoral purpose.
predicates.transfer_not_set_aside_at_heirs_instance: The transfer is not set aside at the instance of an heir.

issues.definition: When an heir challenges a transfer of ancestral land, the transfer is for consideration, the applicable custom permits it, and it was not made for an immoral purpose, the transfer is not set aside at the heir’s instance.

issues.legal_issue: Under the applicable custom, the holder’s power to transfer ancestral land for consideration does not depend on whether the holder has a son.
material_facts: The holder had sons who challenged his sale of ancestral agricultural land.
The applicable customary records did not establish a distinction between a holder with sons and one without sons.
Courts had consistently recognized the power to transfer ancestral property for consideration even when the holder had sons.
The court considered the view that restrictions on alienation, where they exist, rest on an agnatic theory and do not justify distinguishing holders by whether they have sons.
issues.conclusion: The existence of sons does not restrict the holder’s customary power to transfer ancestral land for consideration.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on the customary records and the consistent decisions recognizing the power of holders with sons, and declined to treat the doubt expressed in Joseph’s Customary Law Manual as sufficient to unsettle that settled law. It also referred to the agnatic theory discussed in Gujar v. Sham Das. Budal v. Kirpa Ram was not followed because it had not been followed in later decisions and was an unsatisfactory authority.

predicates.holder_has_sons: The holder of ancestral land has one or more sons.
predicates.customary_transfer_power: The applicable custom permits the holder to transfer the ancestral land for consideration.
predicates.transfer_for_consideration: The holder transferred the land in exchange for consideration.
predicates.sons_do_not_limit_transfer_power: The holder’s sons do not restrict the holder’s power to make the transfer.

issues.definition: If a holder has sons and the applicable custom permits a transfer of ancestral land for consideration, the sons do not restrict that power.
